paper_title: Exact solution for the collective non-Markovian decay of two fully excited quantum emitters (Lanuza, 2024, arXiv)
deeper_reasoning_1:
\section*{Claim}
The solved transformed amplitudes are an exact solution certificate for the original two-excitation initial-value problem.  More precisely, if the parity functions \(C_\sigma(\omega,z)\) satisfy the secular equation, if \(C(\omega,z)\) is reconstructed from the parity identity, and if \(\widetilde A,\widetilde B_{p,q},\widetilde B_{q,q},\widetilde C_{m,q}\) are then reconstructed by the transformed Schrodinger equations, then the inverse Wick-rotated Laplace transform gives the unique trajectory generated by the Hamiltonian from \(\widehat a_1^\dagger\widehat a_2^\dagger\vert0\rangle\).

\section*{Premises}
\begin{align*}
\text{(P1)}\quad & [\widehat N,\widehat H]=0,\qquad
\widehat N\vert\psi(0)\rangle=2\vert\psi(0)\rangle,\\
\text{(P2)}\quad & \mathcal H_2=\operatorname{span}\{\widehat a_1^\dagger\widehat a_2^\dagger\vert0\rangle,
\widehat b_j^\dagger\widehat b_{j'}^\dagger\vert0\rangle,
(1/\sqrt2)\widehat b_j^\dagger\widehat b_j^\dagger\vert0\rangle,
\widehat a_m^\dagger\widehat b_j^\dagger\vert0\rangle\},\\
\text{(P3)}\quad & \vert\psi(t)\rangle=A(t)\widehat a_1^\dagger\widehat a_2^\dagger\vert0\rangle
+\sum_{j<j'}B_{j,j'}(t)\widehat b_j^\dagger\widehat b_{j'}^\dagger\vert0\rangle
+\sum_j B_{j,j}(t)(1/\sqrt2)\widehat b_j^\dagger\widehat b_j^\dagger\vert0\rangle
+\sum_{m,j}C_{m,j}(t)\widehat a_m^\dagger\widehat b_j^\dagger\vert0\rangle,\\
\text{(P4)}\quad & C_\sigma(\omega,z)=\frac{1}{2}\left(C(\omega,z)+\sigma z^{-1}C(\omega,z^{-1})\right),\qquad
C_\sigma(\omega,z^{-1})=\sigma zC_\sigma(\omega,z),\\
\text{(P5)}\quad & C_\sigma(\omega,z)\text{ satisfies the parity-resolved secular equation with }
\delta\omega=\omega+\frac{z+z^{-1}}{2}\text{ and }\widetilde a_\sigma(\delta\omega),\\
\text{(P6)}\quad & \widetilde A,\widetilde B_{p,q},\widetilde B_{q,q},\widetilde C_{m,q}
\text{ are reconstructed from }C_\sigma\text{ by the transformed equations},\\
\text{(P7)}\quad & \widetilde X(\omega):=(\widetilde A,\widetilde B,\widetilde C)(\omega)
\text{ satisfies }(\omega-\widehat H_2/\hbar)\widetilde X(\omega)=X_0,\\
\text{(P8)}\quad & X(t)=-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{-\infty+i0^+}^{+\infty+i0^+}\widetilde X(\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\,d\omega,\\
\text{(P9)}\quad & \text{On the chosen transform class, the inverse transform is injective and differentiating under the contour is valid.}
\end{align*}

\section*{Derivation}
By (P1), the exact evolution never leaves \(\mathcal H_2\).  Therefore the coefficient vector \(X(t)\) in (P3) is a complete coordinate description of the state.  Taking the Wick-rotated Laplace transform of the coefficient equations induced by \(\widehat H\) gives a linear resolvent equation of the form
\[
(\omega-\widehat H_2/\hbar)\widetilde X(\omega)=X_0 .
\]
By (P5) and (P6), the constructed amplitudes satisfy exactly this transformed equation, so (P7) holds for the constructed vector.

Now apply the inverse transform (P8).  Using (P9),
\begin{align*}
i\frac{d}{dt}X(t)
&=-\frac{i}{2\pi i}\int_{-\infty+i0^+}^{+\infty+i0^+}(-i\omega)\widetilde X(\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\,d\omega\\
&=-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{-\infty+i0^+}^{+\infty+i0^+}\omega\widetilde X(\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\,d\omega .
\end{align*}
From (P7),
\[
\omega\widetilde X(\omega)=\widehat H_2\widetilde X(\omega)/\hbar+X_0 .
\]
For \(t>0\), the inverse transform of the constant source \(X_0\) gives no bulk contribution, while it fixes the jump at \(t=0\).  Hence
\begin{align*}
i\frac{d}{dt}X(t)
&=\frac{\widehat H_2}{\hbar}\left(-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{-\infty+i0^+}^{+\infty+i0^+}\widetilde X(\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\,d\omega\right)\\
&=\frac{\widehat H_2}{\hbar}X(t).
\end{align*}
The source vector \(X_0\) is the coordinate vector of \(\widehat a_1^\dagger\widehat a_2^\dagger\vert0\rangle\), so the same transform equation also gives
\[
X(0)=X_0 .
\]
Therefore the inverse-transformed coefficients solve the original Schrodinger initial-value problem in \(\mathcal H_2\).  By uniqueness of the linear Hamiltonian evolution, the reconstructed state is the exact trajectory.

\section*{Final Result}
\[
\boxed{
C_\sigma\text{ solving the secular equation}
\Longrightarrow
(\widetilde A,\widetilde B,\widetilde C)\text{ solve the transformed Schrodinger equations}
\Longrightarrow
\vert\psi(t)\rangle\text{ is the exact two-excitation trajectory.}}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
deeper_reasoning_2:
\section*{Claim}
The paper's analytic construction is high-value because the two nontrivial continuations in \(z\), namely inversion \(z\mapsto z^{-1}\) and substitution \(z\mapsto\zeta(\omega,z)\), generate a closed branch orbit.  This closure turns the infinite contour-coupled problem for \(C_\sigma(\omega,z)\) into a finite jump-and-remainder problem.

\section*{Premises}
\begin{align*}
\text{(P1)}\quad & \delta\omega(\omega,z):=\omega+\frac{z+z^{-1}}{2},\\
\text{(P2)}\quad & \zeta^{\pm1}(\omega,z)=-\delta\omega(\omega,z)
\pm\sqrt{\delta\omega(\omega,z)+1}\sqrt{\delta\omega(\omega,z)-1},\\
\text{(P3)}\quad & \zeta(\omega,z^{-1})=\zeta(\omega,z),\\
\text{(P4)}\quad & u=\zeta^{\pm1}(\omega,z)\Longrightarrow
1+2\delta\omega(\omega,u)x+x^2=(x-z)(x-z^{-1}),\\
\text{(P5)}\quad & C_\sigma(\omega,z^{-1})=\sigma zC_\sigma(\omega,z),\qquad \sigma\in\{-1,+1\},\\
\text{(P6)}\quad & \delta^2C_\sigma(z)=\delta C_\sigma(z)-\sigma z^{-1}\delta C_\sigma(z^{-1}),\\
\text{(P7)}\quad & C_\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{2}\delta^2C_\sigma(z)\left(\Phi(z)+\frac{1}{2}\right)
-\frac{1}{2}\delta C_\sigma(z)+\frac{1}{2}r_\sigma(z),\\
\text{(P8)}\quad & r_\sigma(z)\text{ is meromorphic with only the finite pole set introduced by the reconstructed residue equations.}
\end{align*}

\section*{Derivation}
Let
\[
I(z):=z^{-1},\qquad Z(z):=\zeta(\omega,z).
\]
By (P3),
\[
ZI(z)=\zeta(\omega,z^{-1})=\zeta(\omega,z)=Z(z).
\]
By (P4), if \(u=Z(z)\), then the next mobile-pole equation has roots \(z\) and \(z^{-1}\).  Hence
\[
Z(Z(z))\in\{z,z^{-1}\}=\{z,I(z)\}.
\]
Since \(I(I(z))=z\), the orbit generated by \(I\) and \(Z\) from a generic point is contained in
\[
\mathcal O(z)=\{z,z^{-1},\zeta(\omega,z),\zeta(\omega,z)^{-1}\}.
\]
Thus repeated substitution does not generate an infinite tree of new branch locations.

The same closure controls the jumps of \(C_\sigma\).  The first crossing contributes \(\delta C_\sigma(z)\).  The inverted crossing is not independent because (P5) gives
\[
\delta C_\sigma(z^{-1})\mapsto \sigma z^{-1}\delta C_\sigma(z^{-1})
\]
when pulled back to the \(z\)-sheet.  Therefore the net two-cut jump is exactly
\[
\delta^2C_\sigma(z)=\delta C_\sigma(z)-\sigma z^{-1}\delta C_\sigma(z^{-1})
\]
by (P6).  Substituting this jump into (P7) isolates all non-meromorphic sheet dependence in the known factor
\[
\delta^2C_\sigma(z)\left(\Phi(z)+\frac{1}{2}\right)
\]
and leaves \(r_\sigma(z)\).  By (P8), \(r_\sigma\) is determined by finitely many residues and cancellation conditions rather than by a new continuum of unknown boundary data.

\section*{Final Result}
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal O(z)\subseteq\{z,z^{-1},\zeta(\omega,z),\zeta(\omega,z)^{-1}\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
C_\sigma=\frac{1}{2}\delta^2C_\sigma\left(\Phi+\frac{1}{2}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\delta C_\sigma+\frac{1}{2}r_\sigma .
}
\]
Thus the branch geometry is finite, and the secular equation becomes an exact finite analytic reconstruction problem.
\hfill$\blacksquare$
deeper_reasoning_3:
\section*{Claim}
The closed amplitude
\[
\widetilde A(\omega)=\frac{S_1(\omega)^2-S_0(\omega)^2}{2gS_0(\omega)}
\]
is not merely a compact formula: it is a spectral classifier.  Its denominator detects two-excitation bound-state poles, while the endpoint structure of the one-free and two-free continua gives the branch-point set controlling continuum decay.

\section*{Premises}
\begin{align*}
\text{(P1)}\quad & S_0(\omega):=\sum_{\sigma,i}\alpha_\sigma(\omega,z_{\sigma i}),\qquad
S_1(\omega):=\sum_{\sigma,i}\sigma\alpha_\sigma(\omega,z_{\sigma i}),\\
\text{(P2)}\quad & \widetilde A(\omega)=\frac{S_1(\omega)^2-S_0(\omega)^2}{2gS_0(\omega)},\qquad g>0,\\
\text{(P3)}\quad & S_0(\omega_b)=0,\qquad S_0'(\omega_b)\ne0,\qquad S_1(\omega_b)\ne0,\qquad \omega_b\in\mathbb R,\\
\text{(P4)}\quad & S_0(\omega)=S_0'(\omega_b)(\omega-\omega_b)+O((\omega-\omega_b)^2),\\
\text{(P5)}\quad & S_1(\omega)^2-S_0(\omega)^2=S_1(\omega_b)^2+O(\omega-\omega_b),\\
\text{(P6)}\quad & \epsilon_{\sigma i}\text{ is a one-excitation bound-state energy and }\varepsilon\in[-1,1]\text{ is one free-waveguide energy},\\
\text{(P7)}\quad & \varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\in[-1,1]\text{ are two free-waveguide energies},\\
\text{(P8)}\quad & \text{A real physical-sheet pole gives a bound state; a continuum endpoint gives a branch-point candidate.}
\end{align*}

\section*{Derivation}
First consider a zero of \(S_0\).  By (P2), (P4), and (P5),
\begin{align*}
\widetilde A(\omega)
&=\frac{S_1(\omega_b)^2+O(\omega-\omega_b)}
{2gS_0'(\omega_b)(\omega-\omega_b)+O((\omega-\omega_b)^2)}\\
&=\frac{S_1(\omega_b)^2}{2gS_0'(\omega_b)}\frac{1}{\omega-\omega_b}+O(1).
\end{align*}
Thus an uncancelled simple zero of \(S_0\) is a simple pole of \(\widetilde A\).  Since \(\omega_b\) is real and on the physical sheet, (P8) identifies it as a two-excitation bound-state frequency.

Now consider continuum thresholds.  The bound-plus-free energy has the form
\[
E_{\rm bf}=\epsilon_{\sigma i}+\varepsilon .
\]
Using (P6),
\[
-1\le\varepsilon\le1
\Longrightarrow
\epsilon_{\sigma i}-1\le E_{\rm bf}\le \epsilon_{\sigma i}+1.
\]
Hence
\[
E_{\rm bf}\in[\epsilon_{\sigma i}-1,\epsilon_{\sigma i}+1],
\]
so \(\epsilon_{\sigma i}\pm1\) are endpoints.  Similarly,
\[
E_{\rm ff}=\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2,\qquad
\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\in[-1,1],
\]
implies
\[
E_{\rm ff}\in[-2,2],
\]
so \(\pm2\) are the two-free continuum endpoints.  By (P8), the candidate branch points of \(\widetilde A\) are therefore
\[
\omega=\pm2,\qquad \omega=\epsilon_{\sigma i}\pm1 .
\]

\section*{Final Result}
\[
\boxed{
S_0(\omega_b)=0\text{ simply and uncancelled}
\Longrightarrow
\widetilde A(\omega)\sim
\frac{S_1(\omega_b)^2}{2gS_0'(\omega_b)}\frac{1}{\omega-\omega_b},
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
E_{\rm ff}\in[-2,2],\qquad
E_{\rm bf}\in[\epsilon_{\sigma i}-1,\epsilon_{\sigma i}+1],
\qquad
\omega\in\{\pm2,\epsilon_{\sigma i}\pm1\}\text{ are continuum branch-point candidates.}
}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
deeper_reasoning_5:
\section*{Claim}
The criterion
\[
M:=\sup_{t\ge0}P_{\rm one}(t)>\frac{1}{2},\qquad
P_{\rm one}(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\left(|C_{1,j}(t)|^2+|C_{2,j}(t)|^2\right),
\]
is a sufficient, not necessary, witness that the exact trajectory lies beyond both the independent-excitation null model and the Markovian two-emitter cascade null model.

\section*{Premises}
\begin{align*}
\text{(P1)}\quad & P_{\rm one}(t):=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\left(|C_{1,j}(t)|^2+|C_{2,j}(t)|^2\right),\qquad
M:=\sup_{t\ge0}P_{\rm one}(t),\\
\text{(P2)}\quad & \text{Under independent excitations, }P_{\rm ind}=p(1-p)+(1-p)p\text{ for some }p\in[0,1],\\
\text{(P3)}\quad & (2p-1)^2\ge0,\\
\text{(P4)}\quad & \text{In the Markovian cascade, }P_M(t,\Delta)=
\frac{1-\Delta}{1+\Delta}e^{-(1-\Delta)\Gamma t}
+\frac{1+\Delta}{1-\Delta}e^{-(1+\Delta)\Gamma t}
-2\frac{1+\Delta^2}{1-\Delta^2}e^{-2\Gamma t},\\
\text{(P5)}\quad & \sup_{t\ge0,\ |\Delta|<1}P_M(t,\Delta)=\frac{1}{2},\text{ attained at }\Delta=0,\ \Gamma t=\log2,\\
\text{(P6)}\quad & \text{If an exact trajectory exceeds the maximal value allowed by a null model, it violates that null model.}
\end{align*}

\section*{Derivation}
For the independent null model,
\begin{align*}
P_{\rm ind}
&=p(1-p)+(1-p)p\\
&=2p(1-p)\\
&=2p-2p^2 .
\end{align*}
From (P3),
\[
(2p-1)^2\ge0
\Longrightarrow
4p^2-4p+1\ge0
\Longrightarrow
2p-2p^2\le\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
P_{\rm ind}\le\frac{1}{2}.
\]

For the Markovian null model, (P5) gives
\[
P_M(t,\Delta)\le\frac{1}{2}
\quad\text{for all }t\ge0\text{ and }|\Delta|<1,
\]
with the maximal case occurring at \(\Delta=0\) and \(\Gamma t=\log2\).  Indeed, substituting \(\Delta=0\) into (P4) gives
\[
P_M(t,0)=2e^{-\Gamma t}-2e^{-2\Gamma t}.
\]
Let \(u=e^{-\Gamma t}\).  Then \(u\in(0,1]\) and
\[
P_M(t,0)=2u-2u^2\le\frac{1}{2},
\]
with equality iff \(u=1/2\), equivalently \(\Gamma t=\log2\).

Now suppose \(M>1/2\).  Then there exists a time \(t_*\ge0\) such that
\[
P_{\rm one}(t_*)>\frac{1}{2}.
\]
This strict inequality is larger than every independent value \(P_{\rm ind}\) and every Markovian cascade value \(P_M(t,\Delta)\).  By (P6), the exact trajectory violates both null models.  The conclusion is only sufficient: if \(M\le1/2\), the test is silent rather than proving Markovian or independent behavior.

\section*{Final Result}
\[
\boxed{
M>\frac{1}{2}
\Longrightarrow
\text{the exact two-excitation trajectory violates both the independent-excitation and Markovian cascade null models.}
}
\]
\[
\boxed{
M\le\frac{1}{2}\text{ gives no converse conclusion.}
}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
